nodes.statement: ~ item[(a)] Let X be a threefold with only A_2m-singularities, then Theorem shows that X does not admit KSODsxspace. Because K_-1(X) vanishes, see for example , the global obstructions do not apply in this case. An explicit example is the cubic threefold X in P^4 given by \[ z_4 ( z_0^2 + z_1^2 + z_2^2 ) + z_0^3 + z_1^3 + z_2^3 + z_3^3 = 0. \] It has a singularity of type A_2 at p=[0:0:0:0:1] and is smooth away from p. item[(b)] Let us consider the cubic threefold X subseteq P^4 given by the equation \[ z_4 ( z_3^2 - z_0 z_2 ) + z_2^3 + z_1^2 z_0 - 2z_1 z_2 z_3 + z_0^3 = 0 . \] This cubic has an A_11-singularity at q= [0:0:0:0:1] and is smooth away from q (see e.g.\ ). By Theorem we have that X does not admit a KSODxspace. Also in this example, we do not have global obstructions to the existence of KSODsxspace. We show that K_-1(X) otimes Q vanishes -- with a more detailed computation, which we might include in another paper, one can prove that K_-1(X)=0. Indeed, since X contains the rational cubic scrollfootnoteBy a change of coordinates given by z_0' = z_1 - i z_0 and z_1' = z_1 + i z_0, we see that Z is given by the equations z_2^2 = z_3 z_0', z_2 z_4 = z_0' z_1' and z_4 z_3 = z_2 z_1' in P^4, describing an embedding of a rational cubic scroll inside P^4. \[ Z = \ z_2^2 = z_3 ( z_1 - i z_0 ) , \, z_2 z_4 = z_1^2 + z_0^2 , \, z_4 z_3 = z_2 ( z_1 + i z_0 ) \ subseteq P^4, \] we see by that X has non-vanishing defect, see for example , and by we further conclude that the defect of X is maximal. Hence, by we see that K_-1(X) otimes Q vanishes.

~\label{E:A_11}
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] Let $X$ be a threefold with only $A_{2m}$-singularities, then Theorem \ref{T:GoalNEW} shows that $X$ does not admit KSODs\xspace. Because $\mathrm{K}_{-1}(X)$ vanishes, see for example \cite[Corollary 3.8]{KPS19}, the global obstructions do not apply in this case. 
    
    
      An explicit example is the cubic threefold $X$ in $\mathbb{P}^4$ given by
    \[
    z_{4} ( z_0^2 + z_1^2 + z_{2}^2 ) + z_0^3 + z_1^3  + z_{2}^3 + z_{3}^3 = 0.
    \]
    It has a singularity of type $A_2$ at $p=[0:0:0:0:1]$ and is smooth away from $p$. 

    \item[(b)] Let us consider the cubic threefold $X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^4$ given by the equation
\[
z_4 ( z_3^2 - z_0 z_2 ) + z_2^3 + z_1^2 z_0 - 2z_1 z_2 z_3 + z_0^3 = 0 .
\]
This cubic  has an $A_{11}$-singularity at $q= [0:0:0:0:1]$ and  is smooth away from $q$ (see e.g.\ \cite[Section 2]{All03}).
By Theorem \ref{T:GoalNEW} we have that $X$ does not admit a KSOD\xspace.

Also in this example, we do not have global obstructions to the existence of KSODs\xspace. We show that $\mathrm{K}_{-1}(X) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ vanishes -- with a more detailed computation, which we might include in another paper, one can prove that $\mathrm{K}_{-1}(X)=0$.
Indeed, since $X$ contains the 
rational cubic scroll\footnote{By a change of coordinates given by $z_0' = z_1 - i z_0$ and $z_1' = z_1 + i z_0$, we see that $Z$ is given by the equations $z_2^2 = z_3 z_0'$, $z_2 z_4 = z_0' z_1'$ and $z_4 z_3 = z_2 z_1'$ in $\mathbb{P}^4$, describing an embedding of a rational cubic scroll inside $\mathbb{P}^4$.}
\[
Z = \{ z_2^2 = z_3 ( z_1 - i z_0  ) , \, z_2 z_4 = z_1^2 + z_0^2 , \, z_4 z_3 = z_2 ( z_1 + i z_0 ) \} \subseteq \mathbb{P}^4,
\]

we see by \cite[Theorem 1.2]{MV23} that $X$ has non-vanishing defect, see for example \cite[Definition 3.9]{KPS19}, and by \cite[Corollary 3.8]{KPS19} we further conclude that the defect of $X$ is maximal.
Hence, by \cite[Remark 3.11]{KPS19} we see that $\mathrm{K}_{-1}(X) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ vanishes. 
\end{itemize}

nodes.statement: Let (S, m) be a complete local C-algebra with an isolated singularity and residue field C cong S/m. A resolution of singularities pi : Y to Spec(S) of S is a projective morphism from a regular scheme Y to Spec (S) such that pi is an isomorphism away from the singular point m. For a 3-dimensional Gorenstein C-algebra (S , m) we say that a resolution of singularities Y to Spec(S) is small, if all fibres have dimension at most one. We denote the class of singular 3-dimensional complete local Gorenstein C-alge\-bras (S , m) with a small resolution by S^(3) and define S as the class of complete local singularities S', such that there is an S in S^(3) and a C-linear triangle equivalence of singularity categories opnameD^sg(S') cong opnameD^sg(S).

\label{D:frakS}
    
    {Let $(S, \mathfrak{m})$ be a complete local $\mathbb{C}$-algebra with an isolated singularity and residue field $\mathbb{C} \cong S/\mathfrak{m}$. 
    A \emph{resolution of singularities} $\pi : Y \to \mathsf{Spec}(S)$ of $S$ is a projective morphism from a regular scheme $Y$ to $\mathsf{Spec} (S)$ such that $\pi$ is an isomorphism away from the singular point $\mathfrak{m}$.
    For a $3$-dimensional Gorenstein $\mathbb{C}$-algebra $(S , \mathfrak{m})$ we say that a resolution of singularities $Y \to \mathsf{Spec}(S)$ is \emph{small}, if all fibres have dimension at most one.}
    
  

 We denote the class of singular $3$-dimensional 
 complete local 
 Gorenstein $\mathbb{C}$-alge\-bras $(S , \mathfrak{m})$ with a small resolution by $\mathfrak{S}^{(3)}$ and define $\mathfrak{S}$ as the class of complete local singularities $S'$, such that there is an $S \in \mathfrak{S}^{(3)}$ and a $\mathbb{C}$-linear triangle equivalence of singularity categories $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S') \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S)$.

nodes.statement: By work of Reid , the singularities of type S^(3) are hypersurface singularities, cf.\ CrefReid. They are the bases of flops between smooth minimal models of threefolds. Knörrer periodicity yields triangle equivalences between singularity categories of hypersurface singularitiesfootnoteThis also allows us to reduce the case of odd-dimensional ADE-hypersurface singularities to the case of ADE-threefold singularities in our proofs. defined by f in Cllbracket z_0, ldots, z_d rrbracket and f + z_d+1^2 + z_d+2^2 in Cllbracket z_0, ldots, z_d+2 rrbracket, respectively. In particular, for Cllbracket z_0, ldots, z_3 rrbracket/(f) of type S^(3), the singularities Cllbracket z_0, ldots, z_2l+1 rrbracket/(f+z_4^2+cdots+z_2l+1^2) are of type S. Conversely, using work of Gulliksen all singularities of type S are hypersurface singularities. We give a more explicit description in CrefS:AppendixDetailsOnSing.

By work of Reid \cite{Reid83}, the singularities of type $\mathfrak{S}^{(3)}$ are hypersurface singularities, cf.\ \Cref{Reid}. They are the bases of flops between smooth minimal models of threefolds. Knörrer periodicity \cite{Knoerrer} yields triangle equivalences between singularity categories of  hypersurface singularities\footnote{This also allows us to reduce the case of odd-dimensional ADE-hypersurface singularities to the case of ADE-threefold singularities in our proofs.} defined by $f \in \mathbb{C}\llbracket z_0, \ldots, z_d \rrbracket$ and $f + z_{d+1}^2 + z_{d+2}^2 \in \mathbb{C}\llbracket z_0, \ldots, z_{d+2} \rrbracket$, respectively. 
    In particular, for $\mathbb{C}\llbracket z_0, \ldots, z_3 \rrbracket/(f)$ of type $\mathfrak{S}^{(3)}$, the singularities $\mathbb{C}\llbracket z_0, \ldots, z_{2l+1} \rrbracket/(f+z_4^2+\cdots+z_{2l+1}^2)$ are of type $\mathfrak{S}$. 
    
    Conversely, using work of Gulliksen \cite{Gulliksen} all singularities of type $\mathfrak{S}$ are hypersurface singularities. We give a more explicit description in \Cref{S:AppendixDetailsOnSing}.

nodes.name: KSOD\xspace vs.\ algebraic categorical absorption\xspace
nodes.statement: By the same reasoning as in CrefE:KuzShi, every KSODxspace gives rise to an algebraic categorical absorptionxspace of Sing(X). But the following example shows the concept of algebraic categorical absorptionsxspace of singularities is more general. Consider the Gorenstein weighted projective space \[Y=P(1^3, 3)=opnameProjnolimits(C[z_0, ldots, z_3]),\] where deg z_3=3 and deg z_i=1 else. It has a tilting bundle mathcal T by work of Kawamata . Let C subseteq Y be a curve with an A_3-singularity that does not meet the singular point [0:0:0:1] of Y, e.g.\ C=V(z_0^4 - z_1^2z_2(z_2+z_1), z_3). Let X be the blow-up of Y in C. By Orlov's blow-up formula (cf.\ e.g.\ for a formulation in the singular setting) and Kawamata's tilting result, we have an admissible SODxspace opnameD^b(X)=langle opnameD^b(Y), opnameD^b(C) rangle cong langle opnameD^b(R), opnameD^b(C) rangle for a finite-dimensional C-algebra R=End_Y(mathcal T). These equivalences induce equivalences of singularity categories opnameD^sg(widehatmathcal O_X, s) oplus opnameD^sg(widehatmathcal O_X, s') cong overlineopnameD^sg(X) cong opnameD^sg(R) oplus opnameD^sg(C), where s is the strict transform of [0:0:0:1] in Y and s' is the A_3-singularity of X. The essential image of opnameD^sg(R) in smashoverlineopnameD^sg(X) is equivalent to smashopnameD^sg(widehatmathcal O_X, s). This shows that s admits an algebraic categorical absorptionxspace of singularities. On the other hand, CrefT:Main will show that odd-dimensional A_3-singularities do not admit an algebraic categorical absorptionxspace of singularities. In particular, s' does not admit an algebraic categorical absorptionxspace of singularities and therefore X cannot have a KSODxspace.

\label{E:KSOD}
By the same reasoning as in \Cref{E:KuzShi}, every KSOD\xspace gives rise to an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of $\mathsf{Sing}(X)$.
But the following example shows the concept of algebraic categorical absorptions\xspace of singularities is more general. 

Consider the Gorenstein weighted projective space 
\[Y=\mathbb{P}(1^3, 3)=\opname{Proj}\nolimits(\mathbb{C}[z_0, \ldots, z_3]),\] 
where $\deg z_3=3$ and $\deg z_i=1$ else.
It has a tilting bundle ${\mathcal T}$ by work of Kawamata \cite{Kaw21}. 
Let $C \subseteq Y$ be a curve with an $A_3$-singularity that does not meet the singular point $[0:0:0:1]$ of $Y$, e.g.\ $C=V(z_0^4 - z_1^2z_2(z_2+z_1), z_3)$.
Let $X$ be the blow-up of $Y$ in $C$.
By Orlov's blow-up formula (cf.\ e.g.\ \cite[Theorem 5.1]{KPS19} for a formulation in the singular setting) and Kawamata's tilting result, we have an admissible SOD\xspace
\begin{align*}
    \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)=\langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(Y), \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(C) \rangle \cong \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R), \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(C) \rangle
\end{align*}
for a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{C}$-algebra $R=\mathsf{End}_Y({\mathcal T})$. These equivalences induce equivalences of singularity categories
\begin{align*}
\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_{X, s}) \oplus  \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_{X, s'})   \cong \overline{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(X)} \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R) \oplus \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(C), 
\end{align*}
where $s$ is the strict transform of $[0:0:0:1] \in Y$ and $s'$ is the $A_3$-singularity of $X$. The essential image of $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R)$ in $\smash{\overline{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(X)}}$ is equivalent to $\smash{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_{X, s})}$. This shows that $s$ admits an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of singularities.
 On the other hand, \Cref{T:Main} will show that odd-dimensional $A_3$-singularities do \emph{not} admit an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of singularities. In particular, $s'$ does not admit an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of singularities and therefore $X$ cannot have a KSOD\xspace.

nodes.raw_latex:
For an irreducible Gorenstein variety $X$, such that its base locus (i.e.\ the base locus of the canonical bundle $\omega_X$) is empty or consists of a finite set of points, it is known that there are no non-trivial SODs\xspace (see e.g.\ \cite[Corollary 3.3]{Spence} together with \cite[Corollary 6.6]{KS22}).
If the base locus is empty, we know that there are no tilting objects (see \cite[Example 4.6]{KPS19}). If the base locus is non-empty, this seems to be 
less clear. 
Note that in this case, our results still obstruct the existence of tilting objects.
nodes.clean_text: For an irreducible Gorenstein variety X, such that its base locus (i.e.\ the base locus of the canonical bundle omega_X) is empty or consists of a finite set of points, it is known that there are no non-trivial SODsxspace (see e.g.\ together with ). If the base locus is empty, we know that there are no tilting objects (see ). If the base locus is non-empty, this seems to be less clear. Note that in this case, our results still obstruct the existence of tilting objects.

The equivalence induces an equivalence of singularity categories opnameD^sg(X) cong opnameD^sg(R). Since the latter category is idempotent complete , there is a triangle equivalence by work of Orlov, cf.\ Crefprop:decomposition opnameD^sg(X) cong opnameD^sg(widehatO_s). In combination with the discussion above, this shows that s is indeed nodal and finishes the proof of the claimed special case of Theorem , cf.\ Step .

\label{prop:reduceabsorption}
   Let $X$ be a projective Gorenstein variety. 
   Suppose $s \in \mathsf{Sing}(X)$ is an isolated singularity such that $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\smash{\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s})$ is connected. 
   If 
   \[{\mathcal A} = \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_1), \dots, \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_n) \rangle \subseteq \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)\]

   In particular, $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_i)$ is already an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of $s$.

\label{D:GProj}
Let $\Lambda$ be an Gorenstein ring. We define the subcategory
\[
\opname{GP}(\Lambda):=\{X\in\opname{mod}\nolimits\Lambda\mid \mathsf{Ext}^i_\Lambda(X,\Lambda)=0\mbox{ for any }i>0\}
\]
of $\opname{mod}\nolimits\Lambda$. This category is called the category of \emph{Gorenstein projective} $\Lambda$-modules\footnote{If $\Lambda$ is a commutative local Gorenstein ring, then the Gorenstein projective $\Lambda$-modules are precisely the maximal Cohen--Macaulay $\Lambda$-modules.}. 
The \emph{stable category} $\underline{\opname{GP}}_{\opname{proj}\nolimits \Lambda}(\Lambda)$ of $\opname{GP}_{\opname{proj}\nolimits \Lambda}(\Lambda)$ is defined as the additive quotient
\[
   \underline{\opname{GP}}_{\opname{proj}\nolimits \Lambda}(\Lambda):=\frac{\opname{GP}(\Lambda)}{\opname{proj}\nolimits \Lambda},
\]
where $\opname{proj}\nolimits \Lambda$ is the category of finitely generated projective $\Lambda$-modules, see also \Cref{Not:frobenius}. 
The stable category $\underline{\opname{GP}}_{\opname{proj}\nolimits \Lambda}(\Lambda)$ naturally carries a triangulated structure by work of Happel, see \cite{Happel} and \Cref{Not:frobenius}.

\label{defn:ctsmall}
   Let ${\mathcal C}$ be a $2$-Calabi--Yau triangulated category.
   We say $T \in {\mathcal C}$ is a \emph{cluster-tilting object} if
\begin{enumerate}[label={{(\alph*)}}]
   \item ${\mathcal C}(T, \Sigma T)=0$, and
   \item if $X$ is an object such that ${\mathcal C}(T, \Sigma X)=0$ then $X \in \mathsf{add} T$.
\end{enumerate}

As mathcal A_i is idempotent complete, it is closed under summands in mathcal C. In particular, if X = X_1 oplus X_2 is a decomposition of X in mathcal A_i for some 1 leq i leq n with X_j in mathcal C_j then X_j in mathcal A_i,j. As mathcal A_i subseteq mathcal C_1 oplus mathcal C_2 this shows mathcal A_i = mathcal A_i,1 oplus mathcal A_i,2 as triangulated categories. : We have mathcal A coloneqq langle mathcal A_1, dots, mathcal A_n rangle = langle mathcal A_1,1, mathcal A_1,2, dots, mathcal A_n,1, mathcal A_n,2, rangle as we have in particular mathcal A_i = langle mathcal A_i,1, mathcal A_i,2 rangle for 1 leq i leq n by . Rearranging the terms shows that mathcal A = langle langle mathcal A_1,1, dots, mathcal A_n,1 rangle, langle mathcal A_1,2, dots, mathcal A_n,2 rangle rangle and this decomposition is actually orthogonal as any subcategory of mathcal C_1 is orthogonal to any subcategory of mathcal C_2. Note that rearranging the SOD this way does not require that the components mathcal A_i,j are admissible since mathcal A_i,1 and mathcal A_j,2 are orthogonal to each other for 1 leq i,j leq n. It follows from mathcal C_1 subseteq mathcal A that mathcal C_1 subseteq langle mathcal A_1,1, dots, mathcal A_1,n rangle. The other inclusion is trivial as mathcal C_1 subseteq mathcal C is triangulated. : We have 0 = Hom_mathcal C_1(Sigma^-d Y, X)^ast cong Hom_Bbbk(Hom_mathcal C_1(X, Y), Bbbk) for any X in mathcal A_i,1 and any Y in mathcal A_j,1 with 1 leq i < j leq n as mathcal C_1 is d-Calabi--Yau and because the decomposition mathcal C_1 = langle mathcal A_1,1, dots, mathcal A_n,1 rangle is semiorthogonal. This shows that the given decomposition is orthogonal, i.e.\ mathcal C_1 = mathcal A_1,1 oplus dots oplus mathcal A_n,1, and hence mathcal C_1 = mathcal A_i,1 subseteq mathcal A_i for some 1 leq i leq n as mathcal C_1 is connected. \ref{item:SODintersectionSum}: It is clear that the intersection of triangulated subcategories is again a triangulated subcategory and that ${\mathcal A}_{i,1}$ and ${\mathcal A}_{i,2}$ are orthogonal for each $1 \leq i \leq n$.
   As ${\mathcal A}_i$ is idempotent complete, it is closed under summands in ${\mathcal C}$.
   In particular, if $X = X_1 \oplus X_2$ is a decomposition of $X \in {\mathcal A}_i$ for some $1 \leq i \leq n$ with $X_j \in {\mathcal C}_j$ then $X_j \in {\mathcal A}_{i,j}$.
   As ${\mathcal A}_i \subseteq {\mathcal C}_1 \oplus {\mathcal C}_2$ this shows ${\mathcal A}_i = {\mathcal A}_{i,1} \oplus {\mathcal A}_{i,2}$ as triangulated categories.

   \ref{item:SODintersection}: We have ${\mathcal A} \coloneqq \langle {\mathcal A}_1, \dots, {\mathcal A}_n \rangle = \langle {\mathcal A}_{1,1}, {\mathcal A}_{1,2}, \dots, {\mathcal A}_{n,1}, {\mathcal A}_{n,2}, \rangle$ as we have in particular ${\mathcal A}_i = \langle {\mathcal A}_{i,1}, {\mathcal A}_{i,2} \rangle $ for $1 \leq i \leq n$ by \ref{item:SODintersectionSum}.
   Rearranging
   
   the terms shows that ${\mathcal A} = \langle \langle {\mathcal A}_{1,1}, \dots, {\mathcal A}_{n,1} \rangle, \langle {\mathcal A}_{1,2}, \dots, {\mathcal A}_{n,2} \rangle \rangle$ and this decomposition is actually orthogonal as any subcategory of ${\mathcal C}_1$ is orthogonal to any subcategory of ${\mathcal C}_2$.
   Note that rearranging the SOD this way does not require that the components ${\mathcal A}_{i,j}$ are admissible since ${\mathcal A}_{i,1}$ and ${\mathcal A}_{j,2}$ are orthogonal to each other for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$.
   It follows from ${\mathcal C}_1 \subseteq {\mathcal A}$ that ${\mathcal C}_1 \subseteq \langle {\mathcal A}_{1,1}, \dots, {\mathcal A}_{1,n} \rangle$.
   The other inclusion is trivial as ${\mathcal C}_1 \subseteq {\mathcal C}$ is triangulated.

    \ref{item:SODintersectionCY}: We have $0 = \mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal C}_1}(\Sigma^{-d} Y, X)^\ast \cong \mathsf{Hom}_\Bbbk(\mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal C}_1}(X, Y), \Bbbk)$ for any $X \in {\mathcal A}_{i,1} $ and any $Y \in {\mathcal A}_{j,1}$ with $1 \leq i < j \leq n$ as ${\mathcal C}_1$ is $d$-Calabi--Yau and because the decomposition ${\mathcal C}_1 = \langle  {\mathcal A}_{1,1}, \dots, {\mathcal A}_{n,1} \rangle$ is semiorthogonal.
    This shows that the given decomposition is orthogonal, i.e.\ ${\mathcal C}_1 = {\mathcal A}_{1,1} \oplus \dots \oplus {\mathcal A}_{n,1}$, and hence ${\mathcal C}_1 = {\mathcal A}_{i,1} \subseteq {\mathcal A}_i$ for some $1 \leq i \leq n$ as ${\mathcal C}_1$ is connected.
    Thus, we have ${\mathcal C}_1 \oplus {\mathcal A}_{i,2} = {\mathcal A}_i$ by \ref{item:SODintersectionSum}.

\label{prop:reduceabsorption2}
   Let $X$ be a projective Gorenstein variety. 
   Suppose $s \in \mathsf{Sing}(X)$ is an isolated singularity such that $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\smash{\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s})$ is connected. 
   If 
   \[{\mathcal A} = \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_1), \dots, \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_n) \rangle \subseteq \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)\] 
   is an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of $s$ then $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\smash{\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s}) \subseteq \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_i)$ is a triangulated direct summand for some $1 \leq i \leq n$.
   In particular, $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_i)$ is already an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of $s$.

\label{proof:prop2.1}
   We have ${\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{sg}} = \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_1), \dots, \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_n) \rangle \subseteq \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(X) \subseteq \overline{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(X)}$ by \Cref{lem/def:asg}. 
   As ${\mathcal A}$ is an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of $s$ and by \Cref{prop:decomposition} we have 
   \begin{equation} \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}_s(X) \subseteq {\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{sg}} \subseteq \overline{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(X)} = \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s) \oplus \overline{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}_{\mathsf{Sing}(X) \setminus \{s\}}(X)}.\label{eq:inclusions}\end{equation} 
   Moreover, $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_i)$ is idempotent complete for $1 \leq i \leq n$ by \cite[Corollary 2.4]{XWChen}. 
   In particular, ${\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{sg}}$ is idempotent complete, cf.\ \cite[Lemma 2.2]{KPS19}.
   Hence, passing to the idempotent completion on the left side in \eqref{eq:inclusions} and using \Cref{prop:decomposition}\ref{item:equal} yield
   \[ \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s) \subseteq \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_1), \dots, \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_n) \rangle  \subseteq \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s) \oplus \overline{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}_{\mathsf{Sing}(X) \setminus \{s\}}(X)}.\]
   By work of Auslander and Buchweitz, we know that $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\smash{\widehat{{\mathcal O}}_s})$ is $d$-Calabi--Yau, see e.g.~\cite[Theorem 4.28]{WemyssLecture}.
   Now \Cref{lem:SODintersection}\ref{item:SODintersectionCY} shows the claim.

\label{defn:modA}
   A contravariant functor $F \colon {\mathcal A} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is called \emph{finitely presented}, if
   \[F(-) \cong \mathsf{coker}({\mathcal A}(-, X) \xrightarrow{{\mathcal A}(-, f)} {\mathcal A}(-, Y))\] 
   for a morphism $f\colon X \to Y$.
   For any additive category ${\mathcal A}$, we define $\opname{mod}\nolimits \, {\mathcal A}$ to be the category of finitely presented contravariant (additive) functors ${\mathcal A} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ with natural transformations as morphisms.

nodes.statement: Notice, in Crefdefn:modA, if mathcal A is a Bbbk-linear category, for a commutative ring Bbbk, and F colon A to Ab is finitely presented then F(X) is canonically a Bbbk-module for all X in A as it is the cokernel of a Bbbk-linear map of Bbbk-modules. Similarly, any map F(f) colon F(Y) to F(X) is Bbbk-linear for any morphism f in mathcal A(X,Y). Hence, F can be canonically interpreted as a Bbbk-linear functor mathcal A to Mod Bbbk. With the above structure one can also easily show that any natural transformation F to G of finitely presented functors F and G becomes Bbbk-linear with respect to this canonical Bbbk-module structure, using the Yoneda lemma. It follows that we could have replaced Ab by Mod Bbbk in Crefdefn:modA and obtain the same category opnamemodnolimits A. In particular, the category of finitely presented functors is a Bbbk-linear category.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defn:sink}
    We say a morphism $f \in {\mathcal A}(X,Y)$ is
    \begin{enumerate}[label={(\alph*)}]
        \item \emph{right minimal} if $fg = f$ for $g \in \mathsf{End}_{{\mathcal A}}(Y)$ implies that $g$ is an isomorphism, 
        \item \emph{right almost split} if it is not a split epimorphism and any non-split epimorphism $g \in {\mathcal A}(Z,Y)$ factors through it, and
        \item \emph{a sink morphism for $Y$} if it is right almost split and right minimal.
        \item We say ${\mathcal A}$ has \emph{enough sink morphisms}  if all $X \in \opname{ind} {\mathcal A}$ admit a sink morphism.
        \end{enumerate}
        The notions of \emph{left minimal}, \emph{left almost split}, \emph{source morphisms} and \emph{enough source morphisms} are defined dually.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defn:covering}
   Let ${\mathcal M}$ be an additive subcategory of ${\mathcal A}$. 
   \begin{enumerate}[label={{(\alph*)}}]
      \item A \emph{right ${\mathcal M}$-approximation}\footnote{\label{theproperterms}These term are also called \emph{${\mathcal M}$-precover}, \emph{${\mathcal M}$-preenvelope}, \emph{precovering} and \emph{preenveloping}.} of an object $X \in {\mathcal A}$ is a map $f \colon M \to X$ such that the induced map ${\mathcal A}(N, f) \colon {\mathcal A}(N, M) \to {\mathcal A}(N, X)$ is surjective for all $N \in {\mathcal M}$. 
         Dually, we define \emph{left ${\mathcal M}$-approximations}\footref{theproperterms}.
      \item We say ${\mathcal M}$ is \emph{covariantly finite\footref{theproperterms}} in ${\mathcal A}$ if every $X \in {\mathcal A}$ admits a right ${\mathcal M}$-approximation.
          Dually, we define \emph{contravariantly finite}\footref{theproperterms} subcategories of ${\mathcal A}$.


    \item We say ${\mathcal M}$ is \emph{functorially finite} in ${\mathcal A}$ if it is covariantly and contravariantly finite in ${\mathcal A}$.
   \end{enumerate}

\label{new Frobenius structure} 
Suppose ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P} = ({\mathcal E}, {\mathcal S}_{\mathcal P})$ is an exact structure on ${\mathcal E}$ with enough injective objects ${\mathcal I}$. 
Assume there is an equivalence $\tau\colon{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}\to{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal I}$ with a functorial isomorphism 
\[\mathsf{Ext}^1_{{\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}}(X,Y)\cong D\mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal I}}(Y,\tau X)\]
for $X,Y\in{\mathcal E}$.
Let ${\mathcal M}$ be a functorially finite, additive subcategory of ${\mathcal E}$ which is closed under direct summands, contains ${\mathcal P}$ and ${\mathcal I}$ and satisfies $\tau({\mathcal M}/{\mathcal P})={\mathcal M}/{\mathcal I}$. 

Then there exists a Frobenius exact structure ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M} = ({\mathcal E}, {\mathcal S}_{\mathcal M})$ on ${\mathcal E}$ with projective objects ${\mathcal M}$. 
Furthermore, ${\mathcal S}_{\mathcal M} \subseteq {\mathcal S}_{\mathcal P}$ is the class of conflations $Z \rightarrowtail Y \twoheadrightarrow X$ of ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}$ whose deflations induce epimorphisms ${\mathcal E}(M, Y) \to {\mathcal E}(M, X)$ for all $M \in {\mathcal M}$.

The Serre functor $\mathbb{S}$ on $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal P}}$ restricts to a Serre functor on ${\mathcal C}_1$ since for a fixed $X \in {\mathcal C}_1$ and every $Y \in {\mathcal C}_2$, we have 
\[0 = \mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}}(X, Y) \cong D \mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}}(Y, \mathbb{S}(X)),\] 
so $\mathbb{S}(X)$ has to be in ${\mathcal C}_1$ as well. 
Similarly, $\mathbb{S}$ restricts to a Serre functor on ${\mathcal C}_2$.

Define ${\mathcal M} \coloneqq \Phi^{-1}({\mathcal C}_2)$ be the preimage of ${\mathcal C}_2$ under the quotient $\Phi \colon {\mathcal E} \to {\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$. 
By \cite[Lemma A.7]{ACFGS22}, we have that ${\mathcal M} \subseteq {\mathcal E}$ is functorially finite and hence there is a Frobenius exact structure ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M}$ on ${\mathcal E}$ with projective objects ${\mathcal M}$, by \Cref{c:changefrob}. 

To show that ${\mathcal C}_1$ and $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}}$ are equivalent as triangulated categories we construct a diagram
\begin{figure}[H]\begin{tikzcd}
    {\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}} & {\mathcal{X}_\mathcal{P}} & {\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{P}}} \\
    {\underline{\mathcal{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}} & {\underline{\mathcal{X}}_{\mathcal{P}}} & 
    {{\mathcal C}_1 \oplus {\mathcal C}_2 \cong \mathrlap{ \ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal P}}}}
    \arrow["\text{incl.}", from=1-2, to=1-3]
    \arrow["\text{incl.}"', from=1-2, to=1-1]
    \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
    \arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
    \arrow["\sim"', from=2-2, to=2-1]
    \arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
    \arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\end{figure} \noindent where ${\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P}$ is a Frobenius exact subcategory of both ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}$ and ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M}$ such that the inclusion ${\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P} \to {\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ induces the inclusion ${\mathcal C}_1 \to \ul{{\mathcal E}}_{\mathcal P}$ of the triangulated subcategory ${\mathcal C}_1$ and such that the inclusion ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M} \leftarrow {\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P}$ induces a triangle equivalence $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}} \xleftarrow{\sim} \ul{{\mathcal X}}_{{\mathcal P}}$.

Let ${\mathcal X} \coloneqq \Phi^{-1}({\mathcal C}_1)$ be the preimage of ${\mathcal C}_1$ under the quotient $\Phi \colon {\mathcal E} \to {\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$.
By the same argument as in \cite[Example 2.63]{KalckThesis}, we see that ${\mathcal X}$ is closed under extensions, kernels of deflations and cokernels of inflations in ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}$ and the inherited exact structure is a Frobenius exact structure ${\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P}$ with projective objects ${\mathcal P}$.
It is clear that $\ul{{\mathcal X}}_{\mathcal P} = {\mathcal C}_1$ as triangulated categories.

The way the conflations of ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M}$ are constructed in \Cref{new Frobenius structure} together with $\mathsf{Ext}^1_{{\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}}(M,X)\cong \mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}}(\Sigma_{\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{\mathcal P}}^{-1}M, X) = 0$ for all $M \in {\mathcal M}$ and $X \in {\mathcal X}$ imply that any conflation in ${\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P}$ is a conflation in ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M}$. As ${\mathcal P} \subseteq {\mathcal M}$ we have that ${\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P}$ is a Frobenius exact subcategory of ${\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal M}}$ and hence the inclusion ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M} \leftarrow {\mathcal X}_{\mathcal P}$ induces a triangulated functor $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}} \leftarrow \ul{{\mathcal X}}_{{\mathcal P}}$ by \cite[page 23]{HappelBook}. 

It is not hard to see that (as an additive functor) this functor agrees with the restriction of the canonical quotient ${\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P} \to ({\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P})/({\mathcal M}/{\mathcal P})$ to ${\mathcal X}/{\mathcal P}$. Because ${\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P} \cong {\mathcal X}/{\mathcal P}  \oplus {\mathcal M}/{\mathcal P}$ as additive categories, \Cref{L:AddIsomorphThm} implies that $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}} \leftarrow \ul{{\mathcal X}}_{{\mathcal P}}$ is a triangle equivalence.

\label{Ex:Conndisconnected}
   Let $R=\Bbbk Q/I$ be given by the following quiver
\[Q \coloneqq \begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&, column sep = 2em]
	1 \&\& 2 \&\& 3
	\arrow["{a_1}", bend left = 2em, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{a_2}", bend left = 2em, from=1-3, to=1-5]
	\arrow["{b_2}", bend left = 2em, from=1-5, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{b_1}", bend left = 2em, from=1-3, to=1-1]
\end{tikzcd}\]
and admissible ideal $I$ generated by the relations $a_ib_i$ and $b_ia_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Suppose ${\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal P}} \coloneqq \opname{GP}_{{\opname{proj}\nolimits R}}(R)$ is the category of Gorenstein projective $R$-modules with the standard Frobenius exact structure.
As $Q$ is connected, the additive category $\opname{GP}(R)$ is connected.
Indeed, this follows since $\opname{proj}\nolimits R$ is connected and every $X$ in $\opname{GP}(R)$ admits a non-zero morphism $P \to X$ with $P$ projective.

The $\Bbbk$-algebra $R$ is a gentle algebra. 
So \cite[Theorem 2.5(b) and (3.4)]{Kalck15} yield triangle equivalences
\begin{align}\label{E:2nodes}
    \ul{\opname{GP}}_{\opname{proj}\nolimits R}(R) \cong \frac{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\Bbbk)}{\Sigma^2} \oplus \frac{\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\Bbbk)}{\Sigma^2} \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}\left(\frac{\Bbbk \llbracket z_0, z_1\rrbracket}{(z_0 z_1)}\right) \oplus \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}\left(\frac{\Bbbk \llbracket z_0, z_1\rrbracket}{(z_0 z_1)}\right)
\end{align}
where $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\Bbbk)/\Sigma^2$ denotes the orbit category of $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\Bbbk)$.

nodes.raw_latex:
The $\Bbbk$-algebra $R$ in Example \ref{Ex:Conndisconnected} appears in KSODs\xspace of singular varieties, cf.\ \cite{Burban05} for curves and \cite{ps} for threefolds. 
    Its singularity category splits into the singularity categories of two nodes by \eqref{E:2nodes}. 
    However, we show below that this splitting is \emph{not} induced by an admissible SOD\xspace of $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R)$ of the form
    \begin{align}\label{E:fdcatabs2nodes}
        \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R) = \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_1), \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_2) \rangle,
    \end{align}
    where the $R_i$ are finite-dimensional $\Bbbk$-algebras. 
    In other words, $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R)$ provides an algebraic categorical absorption\xspace of two nodes, which cannot be refined to obtain algebraic categorical absorptions\xspace for each node separately. 
    
    However, if we allow derived categories of dg-algebras as components, then the following SOD\xspace yields separate categorical absorptions of the two nodes
    \begin{align*}
        \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R) = \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{fd}}(\Bbbk[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)), \opname{D}^{\mathrm{fd}}(\Bbbk[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)), \opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\Bbbk) \rangle,
    \end{align*}
where $\Bbbk[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ is the dg-algebra with $\deg \varepsilon=-1$ and trivial differential. Such decompositions are studied in greater generality in \cite{KS22a}.

    To see that a SOD\xspace as in \eqref{E:fdcatabs2nodes} is impossible, we note that 
    \begin{align}\label{E:SingK0node}
        K_0\left(\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(\Bbbk\llbracket z_0, z_1\rrbracket/(z_0  z_1))\right) \cong \mathbb{Z},
    \end{align}
    cf.\ \cite[Lemma 2.22]{KPS19}.
    For a finite-dimensional $\Bbbk$-algebra with precisely $n$ distinct simple modules the Gothendieck group of its derived category is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^n$, see \cite[Section III.1]{HappelBook}.
    Furthermore, if it is additionally local of $\Bbbk$-dimension $d$ then the Grothendieck group of its singularity category is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$. 
    
    Hence, $K_0(\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R)) \cong \mathbb{Z}^3$.
    As $K_0$ is additive the admissible SOD\xspace \eqref{E:fdcatabs2nodes} implies $K_0(\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_1)) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ or $K_0(\opname{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(R_2)) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and therefore one of the $R_i$ is local. 
    The admissibility of \eqref{E:fdcatabs2nodes} yields that
    \begin{align}\label{E:fdcatabs2nodes2}
        \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R) \cong \langle \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_1), \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(R_2) \rangle,
    \end{align}
    is admissbile, see \cite[Proposition 1.10]{orl6}.
    Considering Grothendieck groups in \eqref{E:fdcatabs2nodes2} and using  \eqref{E:2nodes} together with Buchweitz's equivalence \Cref{T:BuchweitzIntro} as well as \eqref{E:SingK0node} yields a contradiction.

nodes.statement: Let Q=(Q_0, Q_1) be a quiver. We denote the source and target of alpha in Q_1 by s(alpha) and t(alpha), respectively. For x,y in Q_0 we write Q_1(x,y) subseteq Q_1 for the set of arrows alpha in Q_1 with s(alpha) = x and t(alpha) = y. If Q_1(x,y) neq emptyset we say that y is a direct successor of x and x is a direct predecessor of y. We denote by x^+ and x^- the set of all direct successors and direct predecessors of x in Q_0, respectively.

Let $Q=(Q_0, Q_1)$ be a quiver.
   We denote the \emph{source} and \emph{target} of $\alpha \in Q_1$ by $s(\alpha)$ and $t(\alpha)$, respectively. 
   For $x,y \in Q_0$ we write $Q_1(x,y) \subseteq Q_1$ for the set of arrows $\alpha \in Q_1$ with $s(\alpha) = x$ and $t(\alpha) = y$. 
   If $Q_1(x,y) \neq \emptyset$ we say that $y$ is a \emph{direct successor} of $x$ and $x$ is a \emph{direct predecessor} of $y$.
   We denote by $x^+$ and $x^-$ the set of all direct successors and direct predecessors of $x \in Q_0$, respectively.

[label=(alph*)] item We say Q has no double arrows if |Q_1(x, y)| leq 1 for any vertices x,y in Q_0. item We call Q locally finite if x^+ and x^- are finite for all x in Q_0. item A valuation on Q is a map a colon Q_1 to N_+. We call (Q,a) a valued quiver.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $Q = (Q_0, Q_1)$ be a quiver.
   \begin{enumerate}[label={(\alph*)}]
      \item We say $Q$ has \emph{no double arrows} if $|Q_1(x, y)| \leq 1$ for any vertices $x,y \in Q_0$.
      \item We call $Q$ \emph{locally finite} if $x^+$ and $x^-$ are finite for all $x \in Q_0$.
      \item A \emph{valuation} on $Q$ is a map $a \colon Q_1 \to \mathbb{N}_{+}$.
            We call $(Q,a)$ a \emph{valued quiver}.
   \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: A stable translation quiver is a pair (Q, tau) consisting of a locally finite quiver Q = (Q_0, Q_1) without double arrows and a bijection tau colon Q_0 to Q_0 which satisfies (tau x)^+ = x^-. The bijection sigma colon Q_1 to Q_1 with sigma Q_1(x, y) = Q_1(tau y, x) is called the polarisation of (Q,tau).

The bijection sigma colon Q_1 to Q_1 with sigma Q_1(x, y) = Q_1(tau y, x) is called the polarisation of (Q,tau).

nodes.statement: Let (Q,tau) be a stable translation quiver with polarisation sigma. A valued stable translation quiver is a triplet (Q,tau,a) where a is a valuation on Q satisfying a(sigma alpha) = a(alpha) for any alpha in Q_1.

Let $(Q,\tau)$ be a stable translation quiver with polarisation $\sigma$.
   A \emph{valued stable translation quiver} is a triplet $(Q,\tau,a)$ where $a$ is a valuation on $Q$ satisfying $a(\sigma \alpha) = a(\alpha)$ for any $\alpha \in Q_1$.

nodes.statement: Let mathcal C be a Bbbk-linear, Hom-finite, idempotent complete, triangulated category. Suppose mathcal C admits a Serre functor S colon mathcal C to mathcal C. Let (Q,a) be the valued quiver of mathcal C and tau colon Q_0 to Q_0, \, [X] mapsto [Sigma^-1S(X)] the Auslander--Reiten translation. We call (Q, tau, a) the Auslander--Reiten quiver (AR-quiver) of mathcal C.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defn:ARquiver}
    Let ${\mathcal C}$ be a $\Bbbk$-linear, $\mathsf{Hom}$-finite, idempotent complete, triangulated category.
    Suppose ${\mathcal C}$ admits a Serre functor $\mathbb{S} \colon {\mathcal C} \to {\mathcal C}$.
    Let $(Q,a)$ be the valued quiver of ${\mathcal C}$ and $\tau \colon Q_0 \to Q_0, \, [X] \mapsto [\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb{S}(X)]$ the \emph{Auslander--Reiten translation}.
    We call $(Q, \tau, a)$ the \emph{Auslander--Reiten quiver (AR-quiver)} of ${\mathcal C}$.

We call (Q, tau, a) the Auslander--Reiten quiver (AR-quiver) of mathcal C.

nodes.statement: Under the notation and assumptions of Crefdefn:ARquiver assume the quiver Q of mathcal C is connected. Then the action of the Auslander--Reiten translation tau on objects and hence the AR-quiver (Q,a,tau) of mathcal C does only depend on the underlying Bbbk-linear structure. Indeed, the existence of a Serre-functor is independent of the triangulation and by any triangulation on mathcal C has Auslander--Reiten triangles. We may assume that Q has more than one vertex because otherwise the action of tau on objects is unique anyway. Using that (Q,tau) is a connected stable translation quiver, one then easily shows that at each vertex of Q starts and ends at least one arrow and hence the Auslander--Reiten triangles of mathcal C are non-degenerate. Applying shows the claim.

\label{defn:meshalgebra}
    Suppose $(Q,\tau,a)$ is a finite valued stable translation quiver with polarisation $\sigma$.
    Let $\overline{Q} = (\overline{Q}_0, \overline{Q}_1)$ and $\overline{\sigma}$ be constructed as above.
    \begin{enumerate}[label={(\alph*)}]
       \item The ideal\footnote{We follow the same convention as \cite{ASS} for the composition of arrows.} $I(Q,\tau,a) \coloneqq \big(\smash{\sum_{\alpha \in \overline{Q}_1}} \alpha \overline{\sigma}(\alpha) \big)$ of $\Bbbk \smash{\overline{Q}}^{^{\mathrm{op}}}$ is called the \emph{mesh ideal}.
       \item The \emph{mesh algebra} is the quotient $\Bbbk (Q, \tau, a) := \Bbbk \smash{\overline{Q}}^{^{\mathrm{op}}}/I(Q,\tau,a)$.
       \item A $\Bbbk$-linear, additively finite\footnote{{To define standardness for triangulated categories that are not additively finite }one needs to replace $\Bbbk \smash{\overline{Q}}^{^{\mathrm{op}}}$ by the path category of $Q$ and adopt the definition of $I(Q,\tau,a)$ appropriately.} triangulated category ${\mathcal C}$ is called \emph{standard} if it is $\mathsf{Hom}$-finite, idempotent complete and ${\mathcal C} \cong \opname{proj}\nolimits \Bbbk (Q,\tau,a)$ as additive categories, where $(Q,\tau,a)$ is the AR-quiver of ${\mathcal C}$, cf.\ \Cref{rem:exists,rem:unique}.
    \end{enumerate}

We denote the $\tau$-orbits in the AR-quiver of $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}}$ that we want to remove by $X_i, \tau(X_i), \ldots, \tau^{n_i}(X_i)$ for $1 \leq i \leq t$, set
\[
   X \coloneqq \bigoplus_{i=1}^t \bigoplus_{k=0}^{n_i} \tau^k(X_i)
\]
and define ${\mathcal M}$ to be the preimage of $\mathsf{add} X$ under the canonical quotient ${\mathcal E} \to {\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$.
Then ${\mathcal M} \subseteq {\mathcal E}$ is functorially finite by \cite[Lemma A.7]{ACFGS22} as $\mathsf{add} X ={\mathcal M}/{\mathcal P} \subseteq {\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$ has an additive generator and is therefore functorially finite.
Now, ${\mathcal E}$ admits a Frobenius exact structure ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal M}$ with projective-injective objects ${\mathcal M}$, by \Cref{c:changefrob}.
By construction of ${\mathcal M}$, we have an equivalence ${\mathcal E}/{\mathcal M} \cong ({\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P})/\mathsf{add} X$ as additive categories, using Lemma \ref{L:AddIsomorphThm}. 
As $\mathsf{add} X = {\mathcal M} / {\mathcal P}$ is functorially finite in ${\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$ the conditions of \mbox{\cite[Set-up 3.1]{Jor0705}} are satisfied. 

By \Cref{rem:unique} and \cite[Theorem 4.2(ii)]{Jor0705} the \mbox{AR-quiver} of $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}}$ is obtained from the AR-quiver of $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal P}}$ by removing the vertices corresponding to the summands in $X$ and all adjacent arrows.
Further, $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}}$ is standard by \cite[Theorem 4.2(iii)]{Jor0705} since $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal P}}$ is standard and the AR-quiver of $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}}$ is isomorphic to the AR-quiver of ${\mathcal C}$.
Additively finite, standard triangulated categories with isomorphic, connected AR-quivers are triangle equivalent by \mbox{\cite[Corollary 2]{KellerAmiot}} (see also \cite{KalckYang16}), so there is a triangle equivalence $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal M}} \cong {\mathcal C}$.

\label{C:ReduceType}
Let $d$ be odd and $S$ be a complete local $d$-dimensional ADE-hypersurface singularity such that there is a finite-dimensional Gorenstein $\mathbb{C}$-algebra $R$ and a Frobenius exact structure $\opname{GP}_{\mathcal P}(R)$ which satisfies $\underline{\opname{GP}}_{{\mathcal P}}(R) \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S)$.

Then there is a Frobenius exact structure $\opname{GP}_{\mathcal M}(R)$ on $\opname{GP}(R)$ such that there is a triangle equivalence $\underline{\opname{GP}}_{{\mathcal M}}(R) \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S')$, where $S'$ is a complete local $3$-dimensional ADE-hypersurface singularity
\begin{enumerate}[label={(\alph*)}]
\item of type $A_3$, if $S$ is of type $D_{2m+1}$ (with $m >1$) or of type $E_6$
\item of type $D_4$, if $S$ is of type $E_7$ of $E_8$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S')$ is $2$-Calabi--Yau and $\mathsf{Spec} S'$ has a small resolution, see for example \cite[Theorems 5.7 and 6.2(a)]{BIKR}.

\label{rem:crepant-res}
    A small resolution as in \Cref{D:Small} is \emph{crepant}, i.e.\ $\pi^*{\mathcal O}_S \cong \omega_Y$, where $\omega_Y$ is the canonical sheaf on $Y$ and ${\mathcal O}_S \cong \omega_S$ is the canonical sheaf on $\mathsf{Spec}(S)$ since $S$ is a 
complete local Gorenstein algebra.
We note that, as a crepant resolution of $\mathsf{Spec}(S)$, $Y$ is Calabi--Yau, i.e.\ ${\mathcal O}_Y \cong \pi^*{\mathcal O}_S \cong \omega_Y$.
    
    
    
    
    
     Indeed, set $U = Y \setminus \pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})$. The sheaf $\pi^*\omega_S \cong  \pi^*{\mathcal O}_S$ is a line bundle since ${\mathcal O}_S$ is a line bundle. 

     As 
     the restriction 
     $\pi\colon U \to \mathsf{Spec} (S) \setminus \{\mathfrak{m}\}$ is an isomorphism, we have 
    \begin{align*}
        \pi^*\omega_S|_U \cong \omega_U \cong \omega_Y|_U .
    \end{align*}
    As the resolution is small, we have $\mathrm{codim}_Y(Y \setminus U)\geq 2$, this can be used to show that an extension of $\pi^*\omega_S|_U$ to a line bundle on $Y$ is unique, 
    using the 
    isomorphism between the divisor class groups of $Y$ and $U$ (cf.\ e.g.\ \cite[Chapter II, Proposition 6.5(b)]{hartshorne}). Hence, $\pi^*\omega_S \cong \omega_Y$ showing crepancy.

nodes.statement: For the convenience of the reader, we include a sketch of the argument. We first produce a generator mathcal G of opnameD^b(Y) and then `(partially) mutate' it, to get the tilting bundle mathcal T. Let mathcal L be an ample line bundle on Y. Since pi has fibers of dimension at most 1, work of Bondal--Van den Bergh (cf.\ ) shows that mathcal G=mathcal O_Y oplus mathcal L generates opnameD^b(Y). We next study the graded Ext-algebra of mathcal G. Combining mathcal O_Y cong omega_Y (cf.\ Remark ), with the Grauert--Riemenschneider vanishing theorem shows that R^qpi_*mathcal O_Y cong R^qpi_*omega_Y =0 for q>0 which, since Spec(S) is affine, implies Ext^q_Y(mathcal O_Y, mathcal O_Y) cong H^q(Y, mathcal O_Y) cong H^0(Spec(S), R^qpi_*mathcal O_Y) =0. Since tensoring with a line bundle is an autoequivalence of opnameD^b(Y), we also deduce Ext^q_Y(mathcal L, mathcal L) =0 for all q>0. Now we claim that Ext^q_Y(mathcal O_Y, mathcal L)=0 for all q>0. Since mathcal L is ample, it is generated by global sections and we get a short exact sequence 0 to mathcal K to mathcal O_Y^l to mathcal L to 0. Applying Hom_Y(mathcal O_Y, -) yields a long exact sequence and usingfootnoteSince we have R^>1pi_*mathcal F = 0 for all coherent sheaves mathcal F by our assumption on the fibers of pi, . Ext^>1_Y(mathcal O_Y, mathcal F) cong H^>1(Y, mathcal F) cong H^0(Spec(S), R^>1pi_*mathcal F) =0 for mathcal F=mathcal K and mathcal F= mathcal L shows the claim. Since Ext^1_Y(mathcal L, mathcal O_Y) neq 0 in general, mathcal G is not tilting. However, there is a well-known construction yielding a tilting bundle in this situation. Consider the universal extension 0 to mathcal O_Y^k to mathcal M to mathcal L to 0, constructed from a minimal set of generators varepsilon_1, ldots, varepsilon_k of the finitely generated R-module Ext^1_Y(mathcal L, mathcal O_Y). In particular, this means that the map Hom_Y(mathcal O_Y^k, mathcal O_Y) to Ext^1_Y(mathcal L, mathcal O_Y) to 0 induced by is surjective. In combination with the Ext-vanishing between mathcal L and mathcal O_Y that we have established above and with Ext^>1_Y(mathcal L, mathcal O_Y) cong Ext^>1_Y(mathcal O_Y, mathcal L^-1) = 0 (by ), this implies that Ext^>0_Y(mathcal O_Y oplus mathcal M, mathcal O_Y oplus mathcal M) =0, cf.\ e.g.\ . Hence, mathcal T cong mathcal O_Y oplus mathcal M is tilting, completing the proof.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{D:NCCR} Let $S$ be as in \Cref{Set:VdB}. The $\mathbb{C}$-algebra $\Lambda=\mathsf{End}_S(M)$ is a  \emph{noncommutative crepant resolution (NCCR)} of $S$ if
\begin{enumerate}[label={(\alph*)}]
    \item $M$ is a reflexive\footnote{Since $S$ is Gorenstein, all maximal Cohen--Macaulay $S$-modules are reflexive.} $S$-module.
    \item The $\mathbb{C}$-algebra $\Lambda$ is maximal Cohen--Macaulay as an $S$-module.
    \item $\mathsf{gl.dim} \Lambda < \infty$.
\end{enumerate}

Since Y is regular and since Y has enough locally free sheaves, see Remark , we have Perf(Y) = opnameD^b(Y) and, using the tilting equivalence CrefT:VdB and , we deduce Perf(Lambda) = opnameD^b(Lambda). nodes.raw_latex:
This follows from Theorem 8.18(1) in Iyama--Reiten \cite{IyamaReiten}, for the convenience of the reader, we translate their statement into our setting. 

Firstly, we take $\Lambda=S$ in their statement -- we note that $S$ is $3$-$CY^-$ by \cite[Proposition 3.10]{IyamaReiten}, since $S$ is local Gorenstein and of Krull dimension $3$.

Now, \cite[Lemma 2.23]{IyamaWemyss14} shows that condition (2) in the definition of an NCCR in \cite[page 1138]{IyamaReiten} is satisfied by NCCRs as in Definition \ref{D:NCCR}. Their condition (1) holds since for Gorenstein rings $S$ maximal Cohen--Macaulay modules $M$ are reflexive. Moreover, we show that $M_\mathfrak{p}$ is free for all height one prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}\subseteq S$, in particular, it is a generator. Firstly, $M_\mathfrak{p}$ is maximal Cohen--Macaulay for any prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq S$. Since $S$ has isolated singularities $S_\mathfrak{p}$ is regular for all height one prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$. As the only maximal Cohen--Macaulay modules over regular local rings are free, we have shown that NCCRs in our sense are NCCRs in the sense of \cite[page 1138]{IyamaReiten}.

Thus \cite[Theorem 8.18(1)]{IyamaReiten} shows that $M$ is a maximal $1$-orthogonal $S$-module in $\mathsf{MCM}(S)$, cf.\ \cite[page 1143]{IyamaReiten}. Using Buchweitz's equivalence $\ul{\mathsf{MCM}}(S) \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S)$ and the fact that $\ul{\mathsf{Hom}}_S(\Omega(X), Y) \cong \mathsf{Ext}^1_S(X, Y)$ for $X, Y \in \mathsf{MCM}(S)$ shows that $M$ defines a cluster-tilting object in $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S)$.

The vertices of Q are in bijection with the simple ulA-modules. The number of arrows from vertex i to vertex j is equal to the dimension of DExt^1_ulA(S_i, S_j) for simple ulA-modules S_i, S_j. By definition, ulA cong End_S(pi_*mathcal T)/(e_S) where e_S is the idempotent endomorphism of pi_ast mathcal T which is given by the projection pi_*mathcal T to S to pi_*mathcal T. By CrefL:SerreSub, the simple ulA-modules correspond to simple A=End_S(pi_*mathcal T)-modules that are annihilated by e_S and it suffices to understand Ext^1_A(S_i, S_j) for these simples. Van den Bergh shows that under the equivalence the simple A-modules S_i annihilated by e_S correspond to shifts of sheaves Sigmamathcal O_C_i(-1) on the resolution Y, where, as above, the C_i are the irreducible components of C, see . Consider the commutative diagram
\begin{equation*}
\xymatrix{
    \{ p \}\ar@{->}[d]\ar@{->}[r] & C_i \ar@{->}[d]^{\iota_i}\\
 C_j \ar@{->}[r]^{\iota_j} & Y} 
\end{equation*}
of regular embeddings.
    By \cite[Theorem A.1]{CKS} there is a spectral sequence
\[
E_2^{p,q} = \mathsf{Ext}^{p} ( {\mathcal O}_{ \{p \} } , \mathcal{E}^{\vee}|_{\{p\}}\otimes \mathcal{F}|_{\{p\}} \otimes \wedge^1\mathcal{N}_{\{p\} / C_j } \otimes \wedge^{1-q} E ) \Rightarrow \mathsf{Ext}^{p+q}_Y ({\iota_i}_\ast\mathcal{E} , {\iota_j}_\ast\mathcal{F} ),
\]    
where $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ are vector bundles on $C_i$ and $C_j$, respectively, $\mathcal{N}_{\{p\} / C_j }$ is the normal bundle of $\{p\}\hookrightarrow C_j$ and $E$ is the excess bundle
\[
E = \frac{\mathcal{T}_Y|_{p}}{\mathcal{T}_{C_i}|_{p}\oplus \mathcal{T}_{C_j}|_{p}}.
\]
In this case, it is clear that $\mathcal{N}_{\{p\} / C_j } \simeq {\mathcal O}_{\{p \}}$ and that $E \simeq {\mathcal O}_{\{p \}}$.
Plugging this in into the spectral sequence and substituting $\mathcal{E}={\mathcal O}_{C_i}$ and $\mathcal{F}={\mathcal O}_{C_j}$, we get
\[
E_2^{p,q} = \mathsf{Ext}^{p} ( {\mathcal O}_{ \{p \} } ,  \wedge^{1-q} {\mathcal O}_{\{p\}} ) \Rightarrow \mathsf{Ext}^{p+q}_Y ({\mathcal O}_{C_i} , {\mathcal O}_{C_j} ).
\]
Thus, we read off that $\mathsf{Ext}^{1}_Y ({\mathcal O}_{C_i} , {\mathcal O}_{C_j} ) \simeq \mathbb{C}$. In particular, 
\begin{align*}

\end{align*}

\begin{enumerate}[label={{(\alph*)}}]

    \item $\opname{ker}\nolimits {\mathcal A}(-,f) \subseteq \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal A}}(-,Y)$.
\end{enumerate}

Because $\mathsf{pr.dim} F < \infty$ we can find a finite projective resolution of $F$ in $\opname{mod}\nolimits {\mathcal A}$. 
    Using the Yoneda lemma we may assume that this finite projective resolution of $F$ is of the form ${\mathcal A}(-, X_{\bullet})$ for a bounded complex $X_{\bullet}$ with terms in ${\mathcal A}$.
    
    Let $P_F \coloneqq \bigoplus_{k\in \mathbb{N}} X_{k}$, which is well-defined since $X_\bullet$ is bounded. 
    Suppose we are given $P \in {\mathcal A}$ with $\mathsf{add} P \supseteq \mathsf{add} P_F$ and $A \coloneqq \mathsf{End}_{{\mathcal A}}(P)$.
    Since $X_{k}$ is in $\mathsf{add} P$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we know that ${\mathcal A}(P,X_{k})$ is a projective $A$-module. 
    This shows that ${\mathcal A}(P, X_{\bullet})$ is a finite projective resolution of $F(P)$ in $\opname{mod}\nolimits A$ and therefore $F(P)$ is of finite projective dimension as $A$-module.
    This establishes part \ref{item:finprdim}.
   
   Let $G \in \opname{mod}\nolimits {\mathcal A}$. Using that $X_\bullet$ has terms in $\mathsf{add} P$ and \Cref{lem:yoneda} the complexes $\mathsf{Hom}_{\opname{mod}\nolimits {\mathcal A}}({\mathcal A}(-, X_{\bullet}), G(-))$ and $\mathsf{Hom}_{A}({\mathcal A}(P, X_{\bullet}), G(P))$ are isomorphic.
   Hence, the two complexes have isomorphic homology, i.e.\ $\mathsf{Ext}_{\opname{mod}\nolimits {\mathcal A}}^i(F, G) \cong \mathsf{Ext}^i_{A}(F(P),G(P))$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. 
   This establishes part \ref{item:extiso}.

    We show that $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are cyclically free, in the sense of \cite[page 2739]{IgusaLiuPaquette}, that is $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are not summands of a \emph{minimal relation} $\rho := \sum_{l=1}^n \lambda_l p_l \in I$ of $A$, where the $\lambda_l \in \Bbbk$ are non-zero scalars, the $p_l$ are distinct paths in $Q$ from $i$ to $i$ and $\sum_{l \in \Omega} \lambda_l p_l \notin I$ for all $\emptyset \subsetneq \Omega \subsetneq \{1,\dots,n\}$. 
    Indeed, if $p_l = \sigma_1$ for some $1 \leq l \leq n$ then $\rho / \lambda_l$ would be of the form $\alpha \beta + c$ where $c \neq - \alpha \beta$ is a sum of paths from $i$ to $i$. This would imply $\mathsf{Ext}^2_A(S_i, S_i) \neq 0$ by \cite[Lemma 3.10]{GLSInv}. Similarly, $p_l \neq \sigma_2$ for $1 \leq l \leq n$. This shows that $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are cyclically free.

Hence, part \ref{item:glsgeneralized2} is true and part \ref{item:glsgeneralized1} follows from part \ref{item:glsgeneralized2} by \Cref{lem:extar}, cf.\ also \cite[Lemma III.2.12]{ASS}.

\label{defn:ct}
   A subcategory ${\mathcal T}$ of ${\mathcal E}$ (or ${\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$) is called a \emph{cluster-tilting subcategory}\footnote{This is sometimes called $2$-cluster-tilting subcategory.}\footnote{In a non-Calabi--Yau setting the definition in \Cref{remark:proj in ct}\ref{item:otherdef} is different and more common.} of ${\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ (or $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal P}}$) if the following conditions hold. 
\begin{enumerate}[label={{(\alph*)}}]
   \item $\mathsf{Ext}^1(T, T')=0$ for all $T,T' \in {\mathcal T}$.
   \item If $X$ is an object such that $\mathsf{Ext}^1(T, X)=0$ for all $T \in {\mathcal T}$, then $X \in {\mathcal T}$.
   \item ${\mathcal T} \subseteq {\mathcal E}$ (or ${\mathcal T} \subseteq {\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$) is functorially finite.
\end{enumerate}
Here, $\mathsf{Ext}^1(-,-) := \mathsf{Ext}^1_{{\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal P}}}(-,-)$ (or $\mathsf{Ext}^1(-,-) := {\mathsf{Hom}_{{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}}}(-,\Sigma_{\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{\mathcal P}}-)$).

Suppose we are in the setting of \Cref{defn:ct}.
\begin{enumerate}[label={{(\alph*)}}]\label{remark:proj in ct}
   \item By definition any cluster-tilting subcategory is an additive subcategory which is closed under direct summands and isomorphisms.
   \item Suppose ${\mathcal T}$ is a cluster-tilting subcategory of ${\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal P}}$.
         Then ${\mathcal P} \subseteq {\mathcal T}$ by condition (b) and the Frobenius property of ${\mathcal E}_{{\mathcal P}}$\label{item:proj in ct}.
         This implies that any left (right) ${\mathcal T}$-approximation is an inflation (deflation) by a similar argument as in the proof of \Cref{lem:exactpd2}\ref{item:exactpd2}.
   \item\label{item:otherdef} One can check that ${\mathcal T}$ is a cluster-tilting subcategory of $\mathcal{E}_{{\mathcal P}}$ (or $\ul{{\mathcal E}}_{{\mathcal P}}$) if and only if it is functorially finite in ${\mathcal E}$ (or ${\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}$) and
   \begin{align*}
      {\mathcal T} &= \set{X }{\text{$\mathsf{Ext}^1_{}(T, X)=0$ for all $T \in {\mathcal T}$}} \\
          &= \set{X }{\text{$\mathsf{Ext}^1_{}(X, T)=0$ for all $T \in {\mathcal T}$}}.
   \end{align*}
   The latter definition is used in \cite{BIKR} in our setting. 
   The second equality follows from the $2$-Calabi--Yau property, see \cite[Proposition I.1.1]{BIRSc} for ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}$.

nodes.statement: We show there is an automorphism factoring through f if it is not in the radical. Suppose \[f = left[ f_1 & f_2 right] colon X_1 oplus X_2 to Y\] is a decomposition then one of f_1 and f_2 is not in the radical, as it is an ideal. Furthermore, if a non-trivial automorphism factors through f_1 or f_2 then it factors through f. As A has the descending chain condition on direct summands, this argument and its dual shows that we can assume that X and Y are indecomposable. As f is not in the radical we have g in mathcal A(Y,X) such that 1_X - gf is not invertible. As End_mathcal A (X) is local that means that 1_X - gf is in rad End_mathcal A( X). So gf = 1_X - (1_X -gf) is invertible and hence an automorphism. The converse follows as radical is an ideal not containing any isomorphism.

We show there is an automorphism factoring through $f$ if it is not in the radical.
    Suppose
    \[f = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} f_1 & f_2 \end{smallmatrix}\right] \colon X_1 \oplus X_2 \to Y\]
    is a decomposition then one of $f_1$ and $f_2$ is not in the radical, as it is an ideal.
    Furthermore, if a non-trivial automorphism factors through $f_1$ or $f_2$ then it factors through $f$.
    As $\mathcal{A}$ has the descending chain condition on direct summands, this argument and its dual shows that we can assume that $X$ and $Y$ are indecomposable.

    So $gf = \mathbf{1}_X - (\mathbf{1}_X -gf)$ is invertible and hence an automorphism.

    The converse follows as radical is an ideal not containing any isomorphism.

nodes.statement: A non-trivial automorphism factors through a morphism f in A(X,Y) if and only if f induces an isomorphism between a non-trivial common direct summand of X and Y. If X and Y are indecomposable this is only possible if f is itself an isomorphism. The first part follows now from Creflem:bestchar. Notice, a non-trivial common direct summand between X and Y yields a non-trivial automorphism factoring through a morphism in mathcal A(X,Y). Hence, there is an automorphism factoring through a morphism in mathcal A(X,Y) if and only if X and Y share a non-trivial direct summand. Again, Creflem:bestchar and Creflem:unique show equivalence of the statements in the second part.

First notice, at every object of $\mathsf{add} X$ ends a radical morphism through which any other radical morphism ending at the same object factors.
    In fact, such a morphism can be obtained as a direct sum of sink morphisms ending at $X$.
    We call such a morphism a \emph{right $\mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal A}}$-approximation}. 

    It suffices to show that $X$ has a right $({\mathcal A} \setminus \mathsf{add} X)$-approximation.
    Let $X_0 = X$ and pick for $i \in \mathbb{N}$ inductively a right $\mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal A}}$-approximation 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:radapproxmation}\left[\begin{smallmatrix} f_{i+1} & g_{i+1} \end{smallmatrix}\right] \colon X_{i+1} \oplus Y_{i+1} \to X_{i},\end{align}
    where the domain is decomposed such that $X_{i+1} \in \mathsf{add} X$ and $\mathsf{add} Y_{i+1} \cap \mathsf{add} X = 0$.
    Since $\mathsf{End}_{{\mathcal A}}(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $\Bbbk$-algebra there exists an $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\mathsf{rad}^n \mathsf{End}_{{\mathcal A}}(X) = 0$. 
    Let $h_1 = g_1$ and $h_i = f_1 \cdots f_{i-1} g_i$ for $i \geq 2$.
    We claim that
    \[h \coloneqq \left[\begin{smallmatrix} h_{1} & \cdots & h_n \end{smallmatrix}\right] \colon Y_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus Y_n \to X\]
    is a right $({\mathcal A} \setminus \mathsf{add} X)$-approximation.
    
    Let $Z \in {\mathcal A} \setminus \mathsf{add} X$ and $k_0 \colon Z \to X$ be arbitrary.
    We have ${\mathcal A}(Z, X_i) = \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal A}}(Z, X_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$ by \Cref{lem:radical}.
    We can pick morphisms
    \[\left[\begin{smallmatrix} k_{i+1} \\ l_{i+1} \end{smallmatrix}\right] \colon Z \to X_{i+1} \oplus Y_{i+1}\] 
    inductively such that $\label{eq:firstfactor}k_i = f_{i+1}k_{i+1} + g_{i+1}l_{i+1}$
    for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where we used that \eqref{eq:radapproxmation} is a right $\mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal A}}$-approximation.
    By induction one shows
    \begin{align}\label{eq:magicfactorization} k_0 = f_1 \cdots f_{n} k_{n} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} h_i l_i = f_1 \cdots f_{n} k_{n} + \left[\begin{smallmatrix} h_{1} & \cdots & h_n \end{smallmatrix}\right] \left[\begin{smallmatrix} l_{1} \\ \vdots \\ l_n \end{smallmatrix}\right]. \end{align}
    Notice, $f_1 \cdots f_{n} = 0$ because $\mathsf{rad}^n \mathsf{End}_{{\mathcal A}} (X) = 0$ and $X_i \in \mathsf{add} X$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
    Thus \eqref{eq:magicfactorization} shows that $k_0$ factors through $h$.

Suppose $\ul{f} \colon Y \to X$ is a sink morphism in ${{\mathcal E}}/{\mathcal P}$ and $g \colon P \to X$ is a deflation in ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}$ with $P \in {\mathcal P}$. 
    Then $g \in \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal E}}(P,X)$ by \Cref{lem:radical} and $\ul{f} \in \mathsf{rad}_{{{\mathcal E}}/{\mathcal P}}(Y, X)$ by assumption. 
    We may assume that $f \in \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal E}}(Y,X)$ by \Cref{lem:radicalfunctor}\ref{item:radicaliso}.
    Then 
    \[h \coloneqq \left[\begin{smallmatrix} f & g \end{smallmatrix}\right] \colon Y \oplus P \to X\]
    is deflation in ${\mathcal E}_{\mathcal P}$, cf.\ e.g.\ \cite[Lemma A.1(i)]{JY22}, and a radical morphism.
    
    If $k \in {\mathcal E}(Z,X)$ is not a split epimorphism then $k \in \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal E}}(Z,X)$ and therefore $\ul{k} \in \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal E}/{\mathcal P}}(Z, X)$ by \Cref{lem:radicalfunctor}\ref{item:radicaliso}. 
    By \Cref{lem:jenny}, $k$ factors through $h$ as $\ul{k}$ factors through $\ul{f} \cong \ul{h}$.
    Hence $h$ is a right almost split morphism ending at $X$.
    It follows from \Cref{setup:algebraicsetup}\ref{ks} that $X$ has a sink morphism in ${\mathcal E}$, cf.\ e.g.\ \Cref{rem:krause}.

\label{thm:IyamaYoshino}
    Let ${\mathcal C}$ be a $2$-Calabi--Yau triangulated category satisfying \Cref{setup:algebraicsetup}\ref{ks}, \ref{hf}.
    Suppose ${\mathcal T} \subseteq {\mathcal C}$ is a cluster-tilting subcategory and ${\mathcal U} \coloneqq {\mathcal T} \setminus \mathsf{add} T$ for some $T \in \opname{ind} {\mathcal T}$. 
    Then there is $T^\ast \in \opname{ind} {\mathcal C} \setminus \opname{ind} {\mathcal T}$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
        \item ${\mathcal T}^\ast \coloneqq \mathsf{add}( {\mathcal U} \cup \{T^\ast\})$ is a cluster-tilting subcategory of ${\mathcal C}$ and
        \item there are triangles
        \[\text{\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
        {T^\ast} \& U \& T \& {\Sigma T^\ast}
        \arrow["f", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["g", from=1-2, to=1-3]
        \arrow["h", from=1-3, to=1-4]
        \end{tikzcd} and \begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
        T \& V \& {T^\ast} \& {\Sigma T}
        \arrow["{i}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["{j}", from=1-2, to=1-3]
        \arrow["{k}", from=1-3, to=1-4]
        \end{tikzcd}}
        \]
        in ${\mathcal C}$, where $g$ and $j$ are right minimal right ${\mathcal U}$-approximations and $f$ and $i$ are left minimal left ${\mathcal U}$-approximations.
    \end{enumerate}

Notice, ${\mathcal C}$ has enough source and sink morphisms as it has a Serre functor, see \cite[Theorem A]{ReitenVandenBergh}.
    By \Cref{lem:sinksubcat} and its dual, ${\mathcal T}$ has enough source and sink morphisms.
    Now, ${\mathcal U}$ is functorially finite in ${\mathcal T}$ by \Cref{lem:sinkcover} and hence ${\mathcal U}$ is also functorially finite in ${\mathcal C}$ as ${\mathcal T}$ is functorially finite in ${\mathcal C}$. 
    This implies that ${\mathcal U}$ is an almost complete cluster-tilting subcategory in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.2]{IyamaYoshino}. 
    By \cite[Theorem 5.3]{IyamaYoshino} there are exactly two cluster-tilting subcategories ${\mathcal T}$ and ${\mathcal T}^\ast$ of ${\mathcal C}$ with ${\mathcal U} \subseteq {\mathcal T}, {\mathcal T}^\ast$. 
    By the same theorem $({\mathcal T},{\mathcal T}^\ast)$ is an ${\mathcal U}$-mutation pair in the sense of \cite[Definition 2.5]{IyamaYoshino}.
    This ${\mathcal U}$-mutation pair gives us an equivalence $\mathbb{G} \colon {\mathcal T}/{\mathcal U} \to {\mathcal T}^\ast/{\mathcal U}$ as in \cite[Proposition 2.6]{IyamaYoshino}.
    As $T \in \opname{ind} ({\mathcal T}/{\mathcal U})$ is an additive generator of ${\mathcal T}/{\mathcal U}$ its image $\mathbb{G}(T) \in \opname{ind} ({\mathcal T}^\ast/{\mathcal U})$ is an additive generator of ${\mathcal T}^\ast/{\mathcal U}$.
    As ${\mathcal C}$ is Krull--Schmidt we can decompose $\mathbb{G}(T) \cong T^\ast \oplus V^*$ in ${\mathcal T}^\ast$ such that $T^\ast \in \opname{ind} {\mathcal T}^\ast \setminus \opname{ind} {\mathcal U}$ and $V^* \in {\mathcal U}$ and as $\mathbb{G}(T)$ is a additive generator of ${\mathcal T}^\ast/{\mathcal U}$ we have ${\mathcal T}^\ast = \mathsf{add}({\mathcal U} \cup \{T^\ast\})$, compare \Cref{lem:radicalfunctor}\ref{item:kspreimage}.
    By definition of $\mathbb{G}$, see \cite[Proposition 2.6]{IyamaYoshino}, there is a triangle
    \begin{equation}\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&, column sep = .9cm]
        {T} \& {V'} \& {T^\ast \oplus V^*} \& {\Sigma T}
        \arrow["", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["", from=1-2, to=1-3]
        \arrow["", from=1-3, to=1-4]
    \end{tikzcd}\label{eqn:triangle}\end{equation}
    in ${\mathcal C}$ with $V' \in {\mathcal U}$.
    Since $V^\ast, T \in {\mathcal T}$ we have ${\mathcal C}(V^\ast,\Sigma T) = 0$, so the canonical inclusion $V^\ast \to T^\ast \oplus V^\ast$ factors through $V' \to T^\ast \oplus V^\ast$. 
    A standard argument shows that there is a direct summand of the triangle (\ref{eqn:triangle}), which is of the shape
    \[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&, column sep = .9cm]
        {T} \& {V} \& {T^\ast} \& {\Sigma T}
        \arrow["i", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["j", from=1-2, to=1-3]
        \arrow["k", from=1-3, to=1-4]
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    with $V \oplus V^{\ast} = V' \in {\mathcal U}$. 
    It follows from \cite[page 126]{IyamaYoshino} that $j$ is a left ${\mathcal U}$-approximation and $i$ is a right ${\mathcal U}$-approximation. 
    Since $T \notin \mathsf{add} {\mathcal U}$ we have $i \in \mathsf{rad}_{{\mathcal C}}(T,V)$. 
    Hence, $j$ is right-minimal using that the Yoneda-embedding of ${\mathcal C}$ maps triangles to exact sequences and \Cref{lem:minradical,lem:minimalfun}.
    This implies that $j$ is a right minimal right ${\mathcal U}$-approximation. 
    Dually, $i$ is a left minimal left ${\mathcal U}$-approximation.
    
    Notice, ${\mathcal U} = {\mathcal T}^\ast \setminus \mathsf{add} T^\ast$. 
    Hence, the other triangle is obtained by reversing the roles of $T$ and $T^\ast$.

\label{R:BIKR}
    Threefolds of the form $P_3/(g + z_2^2 + z_3^2) $ belong to the class of $cA_n$-singularities, see e.g.\ \cite[Proposition 6.1(e)]{BIKR}.
    In particular, all ADE-hypersurface singularities in dimension $3$ are $cA_n$-singularities for $n=1$ or $2$, see for example \cite[Proposition 6.1(a), (b)]{BIKR}.
    Conversely, isolated $cA_n $-singularities are of the form $P_3/(g + z_2^2 + z_3^2) $ for some $g \in P_1$, which follows from Morse Lemma (see for example \cite[Section 11.1]{Morse}).

\label{T:ClassOfSing}
Let $S \in \mathfrak{S}$. 
Then $d:=\mathsf{dim} \, S$ is odd and there exists a $f \in P_3$ such that the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label={(\alph*)}]
\item The threefold $\mathsf{Spec}(P_3/(f))$ admits a small resolution of singularities.\label{item:threefoldsmallres}
\item If $d \geq 3$ there is an $\mathbb{C}$-algebra isomorphism
\[
S \cong P_d/(f + z_{4}^2 + \cdots + z_d^2).
\]
\item If $d =1$, then there exists $g=f_1 \cdots f_n \in P_1$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}[label={(\arabic*)}]
    \item $f_i \in (z_0, z_1) \setminus (z_0, z_1)^2$ are irreducible and mutually prime,
    \item $P_3/(f)\cong P_3/(g + z_2^2 + z_3^2)$,
    \item $S \cong P_1/(g)$.
\end{enumerate}

\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: By Knörrer's periodicity , part is a consequence of part , so we can assume dim \, S=1. A special case of Wiedemann's mbox shows that the AR-quiver of ulMCM(S) cong opnameD^sg(S) equals the AR-quiver of opnameD^sg(A_2n) and in particular, S has finite MCM-representation type. For the convenience of the reader, we first translate our setting into Wiedemann's and then sketch his argument. By a complete local version of Noether normalization (cf.\ ), there is an embedding of C-algebras R:=Cllbracket t rrbracket subseteq S such that S is a finitely generated R-module. Since S is a domain, S is torsion-free as an R-module and hence free, since R is a DVR. This shows that S is an R-order as in . Moreover, in our setting, S-lattices coincide with maximal Cohen--Macaulay S-modules, so the AR-quiver in is indeed the AR-quiver of ulMCM(S). Let K be the quotient field of R, then KS:=K otimes_R S is a field (as it is a domain which is finite-dimensional as a K-vectorspace). Every S-module M yields a KS-module KM:=K otimes_R M. Now, Wiedemann defines the R-rank of M as dim_K(KM). For completeness, we note that the R-rank depends on the fixed embedding R subseteq S -- this does not affect Wiedemann's arguments. Since KS is a field, the minimal possible R-rank of an S-module is dim_K(KS). Next, Wiedemann constructs the AR-component containing an indecomposable MCM S-module M_0 with a loop, see mbox. By construction, all indecomposable modules in this component have minimal possible R-rank, since this is true for M_0 by and since the R-rank is additive on short exact sequences. We note that the key point is that all the MCM modules M_i in Wiedemann's construction have to be indecomposable as they have minimal possible R-rank. Summing up, there is a AR-component where the R-rank is bounded and hence shows that the AR-quiver of opnameD^sg(S) is finite and consists only of the component containing the loop. By construction this component equals the AR-quiver of opnameD^sg(A_2n), cf.~mbox. Now, by , S is an ADE-hypersurface singularity. The ADE-hypersurface singularities in any fixed dimension are completely determined by the AR-quiver of their singularity categories . This completes the proof.

        A special case of Wiedemann's \mbox{\cite[Corollary on page 354]{Wiedemann}} shows that the AR-quiver of $\ul{\mathsf{MCM}}(S) \cong \opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S)$ equals the AR-quiver of $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(A_{2n})$ and in particular, $S$ has finite MCM-representation type. 
        
        For the convenience of the reader, we first translate our setting into Wiedemann's and then sketch his argument. By a complete local version of Noether normalization (cf.\ \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0323}{Section 0323, Lemma 10.160.11.}]{stacks-project}), there is an embedding of $\mathbb{C}$-algebras $R:=\mathbb{C}\llbracket t \rrbracket \subseteq S$ such that $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-module. Since $S$ is a domain, $S$ is torsion-free as an $R$-module and hence free, since $R$ is a DVR. This shows that $S$ is an $R$-order as in \cite{Wiedemann}. Moreover, in our setting, $S$-lattices coincide with maximal Cohen--Macaulay $S$-modules, so the AR-quiver in \cite{Wiedemann} is indeed the AR-quiver of $\ul{\mathsf{MCM}}(S)$. Let $K$ be the quotient field of $R$, then $KS:=K \otimes_R S$ is a field (as it is a domain which is finite-dimensional as a $K$-vectorspace). Every $S$-module $M$ yields a $KS$-module $KM:=K \otimes_R M$. Now, Wiedemann defines the $R$-rank of $M$ as $\mathsf{dim}_K(KM)$. For completeness, we note that the $R$-rank depends on the fixed embedding $R \subseteq S$ -- this does not affect Wiedemann's arguments. Since $KS$ is a field, the minimal possible $R$-rank of an $S$-module is $\mathsf{dim}_K(KS)$. 
        
        
        

        
        Next, Wiedemann constructs the AR-component containing an indecomposable MCM $S$-module $M_0$ with a loop, see \mbox{\cite[Proof of Theorem 2]{Wiedemann2}}. 
        By construction, all indecomposable modules in this component have minimal possible $R$-rank, since this is true for $M_0$ by \cite[Part (i) of Proposition on page 353]{Wiedemann} and since the $R$-rank is additive on short exact sequences. We note that the key point is that all the MCM modules $M_i$ in Wiedemann's construction have to be indecomposable as they have minimal possible $R$-rank. 
        
        Summing up, there is a AR-component where the $R$-rank is bounded and hence \cite[Theorem 2]{Wiedemann} shows that the AR-quiver of $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(S)$ is finite and consists only of the component containing the loop. 
        By construction this component equals the AR-quiver of $\opname{D}^{\mathrm{sg}}(A_{2n})$, cf.~\mbox{\cite[Corollary on page 354]{Wiedemann}}.
        
        Now, by \cite[Corollary 8.16]{YoshinoBook}, $S$ is an ADE-hypersurface singularity. The ADE-hypersurface singularities in any fixed dimension are completely determined by the AR-quiver of their singularity categories \cite{YoshinoBook}. This completes the proof.
